questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: Apply the boundary condition for E at a reflecting surface
questions.stem: A city planner's memo asks why the electric field must vanish at a conducting wall reflecting a radio wave

options.text: The wall absorbs all field energy
Tangential E must be zero at the conductor
The field doubles at the wall

questions.explanation: A conductor forces tangential E to zero at its surface, which is why the reflected wave must cancel the incident wave there. Absorption is not the reason.
questions.hint: Conductor forces tangential E to zero

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Explain the formation of a standing wave between two reflectors
questions.stem: Explain why a standing pattern settles between two reflecting walls in a memo to the planning team

answer.exemplar: Two waves travelling in opposite directions interfere; where they cancel repeatedly a node forms, and where they add an antinode forms, creating a fixed standing pattern.

questions.explanation: Incident and reflected waves superpose with fixed phase relationships at each point. The resulting interference pattern does not travel, hence it stands.
questions.hint: Opposite waves interfere into a fixed pattern

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain skin effect in a conductor at high frequency
questions.stem: Why does a high-frequency current stay near the surface of a copper conductor

options.text: Charge is repelled by the interior lattice
Changing fields induce eddy currents that cancel the interior field
DC resistance drops to zero at high frequency
The conductor becomes an insulator at high frequency

questions.explanation: Time-varying fields penetrate only a skin depth; induced currents cancel the field deeper inside, confining current to the surface layer. Lattice repulsion is not involved.

questions.topic: Skin depth in copper at a low frequency
questions.learningObjective: Compute skin depth in copper at a given low frequency
questions.stem: For copper with conductivity 5.8e7 S/m and permeability mu0, find the skin depth at 60 Hz in metres
questions.explanation: Skin depth delta equals sqrt(2 over omega mu sigma). At 60 Hz, omega is 377, giving delta about 8.5e-3 m. Using frequency instead of angular frequency underestimates by sqrt(2 pi).

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: Determine how skin depth changes when frequency changes
questions.stem: If the frequency is multiplied by four, by what factor does skin depth change

options.misconception: uses inverse linear instead of inverse square root

options.text: It is halved in the square root sense: factor one half

questions.explanation: Skin depth scales as one over square root of frequency, so quadrupling frequency halves the skin depth. Linear scaling would give a quarter.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: Estimate the effective conducting area using skin depth
questions.stem: A round wire has radius 2 mm and skin depth 0.1 mm; estimate the effective conducting area in m^2
questions.explanation: Effective area is circumference times skin depth, 2 pi r delta, which is 2 pi times 2e-3 times 1e-4, about 1.26e-6 m^2. Using pi r^2 overestimates by including the dead core.

questions.topic: Reading a decade table of skin depths
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of skin depths versus frequency and identify the trend

stimulus.body: Skin depth table for copper: 60 Hz 8.5 mm; 1 kHz 2.1 mm; 1 MHz 66 um; 1 GHz 2.1 um. License original.

questions.stem: What does the table imply about current distribution at 1 GHz

options.text: Current is confined to a thin surface layer

questions.explanation: At 1 GHz the skin depth is only 2.1 um, so current is confined to a very thin surface layer. The table shows depth shrinking as frequency rises.

questions.topic: Why halving is the wrong skin-depth rule
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a claim that skin depth halves when frequency doubles
questions.stem: A memo claims skin depth halves whenever frequency doubles; find the error

options.text: It shrinks by 1 over root 2, not one half

questions.explanation: Skin depth scales as one over square root of frequency, so doubling frequency multiplies depth by one over root two, not one half. The halving rule overstates the shrinkage.

questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about reflected wave and boundary condition
questions.stem: Stage one: what must E_tangential be at a conductor; stage two: what does that imply for the reflected wave

options.text: Nonzero; reflected wave is in phase
Zero; reflected wave cancels incident at surface
Zero; reflected wave doubles incident at surface

questions.explanation: Zero tangential E at the surface forces the reflected wave to cancel the incident wave there. Doubling would require the reflected wave to add, giving a nonzero surface field.

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find node spacing from wavelength
questions.stem: Two reflectors are 1.2 m apart and a standing wave has wavelength 0.4 m; how many nodes lie between them excluding the walls
questions.explanation: Node spacing is lambda over 2, which is 0.2 m. Over 1.2 m there are 6 intervals, hence 5 interior nodes plus the two wall nodes; excluding walls gives 5? Wait 1.2/0.2=6 intervals, interior nodes = 5. Let me set value 5.0.
questions.hint: Nodes are half a wavelength apart

questions.explanation: Exponential decay of current density from the surface is the signature of the skin effect. Uniform current would be a flat line.

questions.topic: Skin depth in copper at a low frequency

stimulus.body: Skin depth table: 60 Hz 8.5 mm; 50 Hz 9.3 mm; 100 Hz 6.6 mm. License original.

questions.explanation: Lower frequency gives larger skin depth, so 50 Hz has a larger depth than 60 Hz. The table confirms the inverse square root trend.

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute the new skin depth after a frequency change
questions.stem: If skin depth is 10 mm at 1 kHz, find the skin depth in mm at 4 kHz
questions.explanation: Depth scales as one over square root of frequency, so quadrupling frequency halves the depth: 10 divided by 2 equals 5 mm. Linear scaling would give 2.5 mm.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about effective area at high frequency
questions.stem: At very high frequency, what fraction of a thick wire's cross-section carries most of the current

options.text: A thin annulus near the surface

questions.explanation: Skin effect confines current to a thin surface layer whose thickness is the skin depth. The interior core carries negligible current at high frequency.

questions.topic: Reading a decade table of skin depths
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a reading of a skin-depth table
questions.stem: A planner reads a table and concludes skin depth increases with frequency; find the error

options.text: Skin depth is independent of frequency
Skin depth is infinite at DC

questions.explanation: The table shows depth shrinking as frequency rises. At DC the depth is effectively infinite, but that is a limiting case, not the AC trend.

questions.topic: Why halving is the wrong skin-depth rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the halving rule for skin depth is wrong
questions.stem: Explain why claiming skin depth halves when frequency doubles is wrong

answer.exemplar: Skin depth is proportional to one over the square root of frequency, so doubling frequency multiplies depth by one over root two, not one half; the halving rule overstates the reduction.

questions.explanation: The square root dependence means the reduction is gentler than halving. The halving rule would be correct only for an inverse linear law.

questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find the position of the first E node from a reflecting wall
questions.stem: A wave of wavelength 0.8 m reflects from a conducting wall; find the distance from the wall to the first E node in metres
questions.explanation: The wall itself is the first E node because tangential E must vanish at the conductor. The next node is half a wavelength away at 0.4 m.
questions.hint: The wall is the first node

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about standing wave and reflector spacing
questions.stem: Stage one: what condition must the spacing satisfy for a standing wave; stage two: what results

options.text: Any spacing; a travelling wave results
Spacing is an integer multiple of half wavelength; standing wave results
Spacing is a full wavelength; no interference

questions.explanation: For a stable standing pattern the reflector spacing must be an integer multiple of half a wavelength. Other spacings produce transient or non-resonant behaviour.

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about skin effect and frequency
questions.stem: Stage one: what happens to skin depth as frequency rises; stage two: what happens to current distribution

options.text: Depth shrinks; current confines to surface

questions.explanation: Rising frequency shrinks the skin depth, which confines current to a thinner surface layer. The two trends move together.

questions.stem: A diagram marks the depth at which current density falls to 1/e of its surface value; this depth is
questions.explanation: The depth at which current density decays to 1/e of its surface value is the definition of skin depth. Wavelength and radius are unrelated measures.

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a scaling claim for skin depth
questions.stem: A note claims skin depth is inversely proportional to frequency; find the error

options.text: It is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency
It is directly proportional to frequency

questions.explanation: Skin depth scales as one over square root of frequency, not one over frequency. The inverse linear claim understates the depth at high frequency.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of effective areas and identify the trend

stimulus.body: Effective area table: 1 kHz 12 mm^2; 1 MHz 0.4 mm^2; 1 GHz 0.013 mm^2. License original.

questions.topic: Reading a decade table of skin depths
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about a decade skin-depth table
questions.stem: A decade table shows skin depth dropping by a factor of about 3.16 per decade; why 3.16

options.misconception: uses halving instead of square root

options.text: Because depth is unchanged each decade

questions.explanation: A decade multiplies frequency by 10, and depth scales as one over square root of frequency, so depth is divided by square root of 10, about 3.16. Halving would correspond to quadrupling frequency.

questions.topic: Why halving is the wrong skin-depth rule
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about halving versus square-root scaling
questions.stem: Stage one: how does skin depth scale with frequency; stage two: what is the factor for a doubling

options.text: Inverse square root; factor one over root two

questions.explanation: Skin depth is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, so doubling gives a factor of one over root two, not one half. The halving rule is the common error.

questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the reflected wave in satisfying the boundary condition
questions.stem: Explain how the reflected wave ensures the tangential electric field vanishes at a conductor

answer.exemplar: The reflected wave is generated with the amplitude and phase needed to cancel the incident tangential electric field at the surface, so their sum is zero there.

questions.explanation: The conductor imposes E_tangential equals zero. The reflected wave adjusts its phase, typically pi, so that incident plus reflected equals zero at the surface.
questions.hint: Reflected wave cancels incident at surface

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Numerically find the resonant frequency from reflector spacing
questions.stem: Two reflectors are 0.5 m apart; find the lowest resonant frequency in Hz given wave speed 3e8 m/s
questions.explanation: Lowest resonance occurs when spacing equals half a wavelength, so lambda is 1.0 m and f equals v over lambda, which is 3e8 Hz. Using full wavelength gives 6e8 Hz.
questions.hint: Spacing equals half wavelength at lowest resonance

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in an explanation of skin effect
questions.stem: A memo says high-frequency current stays near the surface because charge is mechanically thrown outward; find the error

options.text: The cause is electromagnetic induction, not mechanical force

questions.explanation: Skin effect arises from electromagnetic induction: changing fields induce currents that cancel deeper penetration. No mechanical force on charge is involved.

questions.topic: Skin depth in copper at a low frequency
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about skin depth and frequency
questions.stem: Stage one: does skin depth increase or decrease as frequency drops; stage two: what happens to current distribution

options.misconception: only at DC, not low AC

questions.explanation: Dropping frequency increases skin depth, letting current penetrate deeper. At DC the depth is effectively infinite, but low AC still has finite depth.

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: Diagram interpretation of skin depth versus frequency
questions.stem: A graph plots skin depth versus frequency on log-log axes as a straight line of slope -1/2; the slope indicates
questions.explanation: A slope of -1/2 on log-log axes means depth is proportional to frequency to the power -1/2, i.e. one over square root of frequency.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the fraction of area used at high frequency
questions.stem: A wire of radius 5 mm has skin depth 0.5 mm at some frequency; find the ratio of effective area to total area
questions.explanation: Effective area is 2 pi r delta and total area is pi r^2, so the ratio is 2 delta over r, which is 2 times 0.5 over 5, equal to 0.2. Using delta over r alone gives 0.1.

questions.topic: Reading a decade table of skin depths
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a decade table of skin depths shows
questions.stem: Explain what a decade table of skin depths communicates to a planner

answer.exemplar: It lists skin depth at frequencies spaced by powers of ten, showing that depth falls by about 3.16 per decade and that current confinement worsens steadily with frequency.

questions.explanation: The decade spacing makes the square root trend easy to read. Each decade multiplies frequency by ten and divides depth by about 3.16.

questions.topic: Why halving is the wrong skin-depth rule
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about the halving rule error
questions.stem: Why is the halving rule for skin depth wrong

options.text: Because depth is linear in frequency
options.misconception: would make halving correct for doubling

options.text: Because depth scales as one over square root of frequency
Because depth is independent of frequency

questions.explanation: The halving rule assumes inverse linear scaling, but the actual dependence is inverse square root. Thus doubling frequency reduces depth by 1 over root 2, not one half.

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in a standing-wave claim
questions.stem: A note claims a standing wave travels slowly between reflectors; find the error

options.text: A standing wave does not travel at all
It travels at twice the wave speed
It travels at half the wave speed

questions.explanation: A standing wave is a fixed interference pattern; its nodes and antinodes do not move. The component waves travel, but their superposition stands still.

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute skin depth at a given frequency
questions.stem: Compute the skin depth in mm for copper at 1 MHz using delta equals 66 divided by square root of f in Hz, with f in Hz
questions.explanation: Using delta equals 66 over square root of f with f in Hz gives 66 over 1000, which is 0.066 mm. The formula encodes the inverse square root scaling.

questions.topic: Skin depth in copper at a low frequency
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about skin depth at low frequency
questions.stem: At very low frequency, what happens to skin depth in copper
questions.explanation: As frequency drops, skin depth grows as one over square root of frequency, becoming very large at low frequency. At DC it is effectively infinite.

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about scaling and a frequency change
questions.stem: Stage one: skin depth scales as what power of frequency; stage two: what factor for a tenfold increase

options.text: Power -1/2; factor one over root ten

questions.explanation: Skin depth scales as frequency to the power -1/2, so a tenfold frequency increase divides depth by square root of 10, about 3.16.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: Spot the error in an area estimate

options.text: Only the surface annulus carries current

questions.topic: Reading a decade table of skin depths

questions.stem: Using the rule that depth falls by 3.16 per decade, find the skin depth in mm at 10 kHz given 2.1 mm at 1 kHz
questions.explanation: 10 kHz is one decade above 1 kHz, so depth is 2.1 divided by 3.16, about 0.664 mm. Linear interpolation would differ.

questions.topic: Why halving is the wrong skin-depth rule
questions.learningObjective: Diagram interpretation of two scaling curves
questions.stem: A diagram overlays the true inverse-square-root curve and the halving rule; the halving curve lies

options.text: Above the true curve at high frequency
options.misconception: would mean halving gives larger depth

options.text: Below the true curve at high frequency
Above at low and below at high

questions.explanation: The halving rule shrinks faster than the square root rule, so at high frequency it predicts a smaller depth than the true value, lying below the true curve.

questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about perfect versus imperfect conductor reflection
questions.stem: For a perfect conductor, what is the magnitude of the reflection coefficient for E
questions.explanation: A perfect conductor reflects all incident energy, so the magnitude of the reflection coefficient is 1.0. Zero would mean no reflection.

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Explain node and antinode positions in a standing wave
questions.stem: Explain where nodes and antinodes occur in a standing wave between two reflectors

answer.exemplar: Nodes occur where incident and reflected waves cancel, a quarter wavelength from each reflector for the first node, and antinodes occur where they add, halfway between nodes.

questions.explanation: The fixed phase relationship between incident and reflected waves creates alternating points of cancellation and reinforcement. Nodes are spaced half a wavelength apart.

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface

questions.stem: What skin depth does the table imply

options.misconception: picks where density is nearly zero

questions.explanation: Skin depth is the depth where current density falls to 1/e, about 0.368, of its surface value. The table shows 0.37 at 0.1 mm, so the skin depth is about 0.1 mm.

options.text: Angular frequency 2 pi f must be used

questions.explanation: The skin-depth formula uses angular frequency omega equals 2 pi f, not ordinary frequency. Using f underestimates omega by 2 pi and overestimates depth by root(2 pi).

questions.topic: How skin depth scales with frequency
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compute skin depth at a new frequency using a reference value
questions.stem: Given skin depth 8.5 mm at 60 Hz, find the skin depth in mm at 240 Hz
questions.explanation: Frequency quadruples, so depth halves: 8.5 divided by 2 equals 4.25 mm. Using inverse linear scaling would give 2.125 mm.

questions.learningObjective: Two-stage reasoning about area and frequency
questions.stem: Stage one: what happens to effective area as frequency rises; stage two: what happens to resistance
questions.explanation: Rising frequency shrinks the effective area, which raises the AC resistance. The two trends are coupled through the skin depth.

questions.topic: Reading a decade table of skin depths
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about a decade table's usefulness
questions.stem: Why is a decade table convenient for skin depths

options.text: Because depth is linear in frequency
Because each decade multiplies depth change by a constant 3.16
Because depth is constant across decades

questions.explanation: Because depth scales as one over square root of frequency, each decade multiplies frequency by 10 and divides depth by square root of 10, about 3.16. This constant factor makes decade tables tidy.

questions.topic: Why halving is the wrong skin-depth rule
questions.learningObjective: Numerically compare halving rule to true value
questions.stem: At 4 kHz the true skin depth is 5.0 mm; what value does the halving rule predict in mm if depth at 1 kHz is 10 mm
questions.explanation: The halving rule halves depth for each doubling of frequency. From 1 kHz to 4 kHz is two doublings, so 10 to 5 to 2.5 mm. The true value is 5.0 mm, showing the rule over-shrinks.

questions.topic: Field at a surface reflecting a wave
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a standing wave has a node at a conducting wall
questions.stem: Explain why a standing electromagnetic wave has a node of E at a conducting wall

answer.exemplar: The conductor forces tangential E to zero at its surface, and the reflected wave cancels the incident wave there, so the total tangential E is zero, forming a node.

questions.explanation: Zero tangential E at the conductor is the boundary condition. Cancellation of incident and reflected waves at the surface produces the node.

questions.topic: Why a standing pattern settles between two reflectors
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about resonance and reflector spacing
questions.stem: For a stable standing wave, the reflector spacing must be

options.text: An integer multiple of half a wavelength

questions.explanation: Standing waves require the round-trip phase to be a multiple of 2 pi, which occurs when spacing is an integer multiple of half a wavelength. Arbitrary spacing gives non-resonant behaviour.

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain the physical origin of skin effect
questions.stem: Explain the physical origin of the skin effect in a conductor

answer.exemplar: A time-varying current produces a changing magnetic field that induces eddy currents; these eddy currents oppose the field deeper in the conductor, confining the net current to a surface layer.

questions.explanation: Faraday induction creates opposing currents that cancel the interior field. The remaining current flows where cancellation is incomplete, near the surface.

questions.stem: A cross-section diagram shades the conducting annulus near the surface; the unshaded core indicates
questions.explanation: The unshaded core carries negligible current because the skin effect confines current to the surface annulus. It is not an insulator or superconductor.

questions.stem: A note states skin depth scales as one over frequency; find the error

options.text: It scales as one over square root of frequency
It scales as one over frequency squared

questions.explanation: Skin depth is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, not frequency. The inverse linear statement shrinks too fast.

questions.topic: How much of a wire's cross-section carries a high-frequency current
questions.learningObjective: Explain why AC resistance exceeds DC resistance at high frequency
questions.stem: Explain why AC resistance exceeds DC resistance in a wire at high frequency

answer.exemplar: At high frequency the skin effect reduces the effective conducting area, so the same current must pass through a smaller region, raising the resistance above its DC value.

questions.explanation: DC uses the full cross-section, while AC at high frequency uses only the surface annulus. Smaller effective area means higher resistance for the same material.
questions.hint: Smaller effective area means higher resistance

questions.stem: Which rule correctly describes skin depth versus frequency

options.text: Depth is divided by root 2 when frequency doubles
Depth is divided by 4 when frequency doubles
Depth is unchanged when frequency doubles

questions.explanation: The correct scaling is inverse square root, so doubling frequency divides depth by root 2. The halving rule is the common misconception.

questions.stem: Stage one: what is the reflection coefficient magnitude for a perfect conductor; stage two: what is the phase

options.misconception: correct magnitude but no phase shift

questions.topic: Why a high-frequency current stays near the surface
questions.learningObjective: Conceptual reasoning about skin effect and resistance
questions.stem: What is the main practical consequence of the skin effect for power transmission at high frequency

options.text: Current spreads through the whole conductor

questions.explanation: Skin effect reduces effective conducting area, raising resistance and losses. This is why high-frequency conductors are often hollow or use Litz wire.

questions.topic: Skin depth in copper at a low frequency
questions.learningObjective: Explain why skin depth is large at low frequency
questions.stem: Explain why skin depth becomes very large at low frequency in copper

answer.exemplar: Skin depth is inversely proportional to the square root of frequency, so as frequency drops toward zero the depth grows without bound, and current penetrates the whole conductor.

questions.explanation: Low frequency means slowly changing fields, which induce weak opposing currents, allowing deep penetration. At DC the depth is effectively infinite.
